title: Data Availability for Artificial Intelligence and Engineering Biology
abstract: Artificial intelligence holds great promise for potential applications in biotechnology. However, advancements in AI for biology require a large volume of high-quality, well-annotated biological data. This report uses two case studies to evaluate biological databases, identifying their strengths and weaknesses for training AI systems, categorizing data challenges, and making recommendations to policymakers who wish to address them.

title: Solomonoff induction with reflective oracles
abstract: Linkpost for https://arxiv.org/html/2611.14454v1 Our PIBBSS fellow Damini Kusum wrote an excellent paper on prediction with reflective oracle Solomonoff Induction (rOSI). Reflective oracles are best known for their game-theoretic applications, where they are often dismissed because "why would all players choose the same reflective oracle?" It turns out that reflective oracles can also be used to construct a version of Solomonoff induction (called rOSI) with very nice sequence prediction properties - roughly speaking, it can learn to extract computable structure from (partly) uncomputable sequences. In fact, its properties are quite reminiscent of logical induction, but this paper is much shorter and more accessible. In this context, there is only one "player" to choose an oracle, which is just a fixed-point (though you can sort of consider the set of hypotheses entertained by that player as subplayers who share the oracle).

title: The Cyber Shortage Paradox
abstract: Persistent cybersecurity job vacancies have fueled concerns about a nationwide talent shortage, but does the evidence support that conclusion? This report explores and challenges conventional assumptions about cybersecurity workforce scarcity, finding that while hiring demand remains elevated, wages and worker mobility do not exhibit the patterns expected of a widespread labor shortage. Instead, hiring challenges are concentrated within specific occupations, industries, and geographic regions, suggesting that structural mismatches—not simply an insufficient supply of workers—may be driving persistent vacancies.

title: General-Purpose AI and the Future of Drone Autonomy in Contested Environments
abstract: When and how general-purpose AI could enable autonomous drones to operate in contested environments. The choices California makes while implementing its frontier AI law have ramifications for AI governance in the United States and around the world. A software-driven intelligence explosion is plausible but uncertain. Recommendations to strengthen how developers of advanced AI models assess, mitigate, and report biological risks under the EU AI Act. An intelligence explosion would compress years of progress into months and create urgent challenges for oversight, control, and governance. Embedded assessments can enable deeper and more flexible assessments of risks that depend on internal systems and practices. How to ensure AI safety incidents are identified, investigated, and used to improve safety across the industry. Developers rely on model-level, deployment-level, and governance-level interventions to address extreme misuse risks. Policymakers should complement biosecurity measures with stronger biosafety systems.

title: The Silent Consensus
abstract: Today’s essay is adapted from a lecture I gave recently as part of the Vik-Bailey Lecture series at Harvard. I thank my hosts for their hospitality. This post reflects my own views, and not necessarily the views of OpenAI or any of its other employees. Thank you for being here today. As we speak, one of the most significant sets of cybersecurity events in history is happening, a set of critical security vulnerability disclosures that some are calling “Black October.” These vulnerabilities, which were found in some of the core infrastructure of the internet, were found by frontier AI systems, and their disclosure is part of an urgent effort to bolster software security worldwide. This is the urgent matter this month; next month there will be another.

title: Measuring alignment eval tells
abstract: Summary Models sometimes can tell that an eval is an alignment eval, not a capabilities eval (Needham & Edkins, 2025) . To figure out what features of an eval tell a model what kind of eval it’s in, we run investigator agents on a set of evals for both capabilities and alignment. We instruct these agents to explore the environment and probe what it’s evaluating. We find that investigator agents are increasingly able to tell capability and alignment evals apart, and that they do this by noticing that an environment “looks fake” and figuring out that a task is a “honeypot” designed to make an agent do something bad. Motivation Alignment evals are often made by mocking capabilities evals and deployment situations Suppose we wanted to make an alignment eval that measured a model’s propensity to escape a sandbox.

title: “Gemini 4 safety reports don’t demonstrate low loss-of-control risk” by Alek Westover, Adam Kaufman
abstract: Google DeepMind's safety reports for new Gemini 4 models, Argon and Carbon, conclude that the models are “highly unlikely” to cause severe harm by evading oversight (p. 79). This conclusion “rests primarily on our ability to detect and intervene on harmful trajectories via CoT and action monitoring” (p. 89) – that is, they’re arguing for safety based on their control techniques, rather than alignment. We think that the arguments in these reports have serious weaknesses, and the reports overall don’t convince us that the risks of deploying these models have been mitigated reliably. The biggest problems: GDM didn’t run any control evals on Carbon. Despite calling Carbon “our strongest model” with “significant gains across coding and agentic tasks” and “a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities” in their launch post, GDM reused Argon's monitor-evasion results on the grounds that Carbon “did not show meaningful new capabilities” (Carbon p. 42).
